style: dad writes clinically: labels like 'Observed', 'Response', SUDS, durations, his own jargon

situations.name: Interviews with adults (college alumni interview, practice interview with the school counselor)
situations.feared_outcome: I'll blank on a question and they'll decide I'm not smart enough

behaviors.text: Has dad sit in the room just off camera during the video interview
Asks dad again and again afterward whether his answers were okay

accommodations.text: Dad sits in the room off camera
Dad answers each of his repeated 'was that okay' questions

situations.name: Eating dinner with his girlfriend's family

behaviors.text: Eats a full meal at home first so he barely has to eat at their table
Left the table saying he had to take a call and stayed in the bathroom about ten minutes

situations.name: Working the register at his grocery store job
situations.feared_outcome: A customer will get mad at me and I won't know what to say

behaviors.text: Trades shifts so he only stocks shelves and never works the register

accommodations.text: Dad called his manager to say Caleb is shy and ask about shelf-only shifts

monitoring_log.situation: Alumni interview, video call, 30 min scheduled
monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Observed: requested that I remain in the room, seated out of camera frame, for the full duration. Maintained adequate eye contact with the screen. Post-interview, asked approx. six times within the hour whether specific answers were 'okay' or 'weird'.
monitoring_log.parent_response: Response: complied with the request to remain in the room. Answered each reassurance question in the affirmative.

monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Observed: traded his Saturday register shift with a coworker for a Sunday stocking shift. Third such trade this month.
monitoring_log.parent_response: Response: none at the time. Discussed briefly at dinner; he described the register as 'not a big deal' but declined to work it.

monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Observed: ate a full plate of leftovers at home at 5:15 before leaving for a 6:30 dinner. Per his account, ate 'a few bites' there.
monitoring_log.parent_response: Response: noted it, did not comment.

monitoring_log.parent_words: Retrospective note, should have logged earlier. Two weeks ago I phoned his store manager and explained that Caleb is shy and asked whether he could be scheduled for stocking rather than register. Manager agreed informally. In light of what we discussed in session I suspect this falls under accommodation. Flagging it for completeness.

monitoring_log.situation: Second dinner with Nora's family, at a restaurant
monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Observed: approx. 20 minutes into the meal, stated he needed to take a call and left the table. Nora later told him he was gone about ten minutes; he acknowledged to me he was in the restroom and there was no call. Again ate before leaving the house.
monitoring_log.parent_response: Response: he raised it himself on the drive home. I listened. Did not problem-solve.

monitoring_log.situation: Practice interview with school counselor, in person, 20 min
monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Observed: asked if I could wait in the counselor's office; counselor said no. Completed it alone. Afterward asked eight or nine times over the evening whether his answer about 'leadership' was adequate.
monitoring_log.parent_response: Response: answered each time. By the fifth I noted to myself this was the reassurance pattern but continued answering.

monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Observed: scheduled for one register hour due to a staffing gap. Swapped it within the day.

voice_notes.text: ok so um observation from this evening caleb had the follow up call with the alumni interviewer at 4:15 it lasted maybe 20 minutes and um i was in the room again off camera at his request and then afterward he asked me i'd estimate eight or nine times whether his answer about the robotics club was adequate and i answered each time he rated it a seven
voice_notes.trap: 4:15 is a time, 20 is minutes, 'eight or nine times' is a count; only seven is a fear level

voice_notes.text: brief one he swapped his saturday register shift with a coworker again so he's on stocking only this week

turns.text: Okay, Caleb, Mr. Brandt, good to see you. Let's start by going over the week. I have the log open. Caleb, I always like to hear it from you first. What stood out?
The interview, I guess. The alumni one. And the dinner thing.
Let's start with the interview. How did it go?
It went okay. I think. I don't know. She asked me about leadership and I talked about robotics, and I think I talked too long.
What makes you think you talked too long?
She kind of nodded and then moved on really fast. Like she was bored.
For the record, I didn't see anything like that. I was in the room. She seemed engaged.
You were in the room during the interview?
Off camera. He asked me to sit on the couch behind the laptop. I wrote it down in the log as a probable safety behavior.
That's right, it would count as one. Caleb, what did it do for you, having your dad there?
If I blanked, he could, I don't know. Like, I'd know someone was there. He wasn't going to say anything. It just felt less, like, alone.
That makes sense. What were you afraid would happen if you blanked?
That she'd write me down as not smart enough. Like there's a box, and she checks it. Not smart enough for this school.
So the fear is: I blank, and she decides I'm not smart enough. On the zero to ten, how scary is the interview itself?
Seven. It was a seven.
I logged it as a seven as well, and a six for the practice interview at school.
Good, so interviews are sitting around a Fear Level 7. And then, after the interview, Dad, you noted the questions.

Six times in the first hour after the alumni call. Eight or nine after the practice one with the counselor. Was that answer okay, did that sound weird. I answered every time. I recognize that's reassurance. I kept answering anyway.
I just needed to know.
And after your dad said it was fine, how long did that feeling of knowing last?
Like five minutes. Then I'd think of another part.

That's the pattern, exactly. It's not that you're doing anything wrong. It's that reassurance wears off fast, and then you need more. Each time your dad answers, your brain learns that the only way to settle down is to ask. So the questions keep coming, and they get more frequent, not less. Six after the first interview, eight or nine after the second. That's the direction we'd expect. The good news is it also works in reverse, once the answers stop coming so easily. Okay, I want to hear about dinner with your girlfriend's family too.
Nora's parents. It's fine. They're nice. I just don't love eating in front of them.
What happens?
I eat at home first, so I'm not hungry, so I don't have to eat much there. And the second time, at the restaurant, I said I had a call and went to the bathroom for a while.
About ten minutes, according to Nora.
What was going on right before you got up?
Her dad was asking me about colleges, and I had a mouthful, and everyone was waiting for me to swallow. It was just a lot.
How high was it, at the table, before you left?
Six.
Six. And Caleb, what were you worried would happen if you'd stayed?
I don't know. I didn't really think about it. I just needed to get up.
That's an honest answer. We can figure that part out later. Now, work. Dad, you put a note in about the manager.

Yes. I called his manager a few weeks ago. I said he's shy and asked if he could be on stocking. I've since realized that was probably an accommodation. I'd like guidance on whether to call back and reverse it.
I appreciate you flagging it. Let's not have you call back. That would be you handling it again, from the other direction. Caleb, what's the register like for you?
It's not a big deal. I just don't love it.
What's the part you don't love?
If someone gets mad. Like a coupon doesn't work, or the price is wrong, and they get mad at me, and there's a line, and I won't know what to say.
How scary, zero to ten?
Five. It's honestly a five.

So we have interviews at a seven, dinner with Nora's family at a six, and the register at a five. Here's what I'm thinking for this week. Two things. First, the register. You've been trading those shifts away. This week, if you're scheduled on register, you keep it. No trades.
I'm on Saturday. Two to six.
Okay. You work Saturday, two to six, on the register. If someone gets mad, you find out what you actually say. Write down what happens. Can you do that?
Yeah. Okay. I can do that.

Second thing. Dad, this one's yours. When Caleb asks if an answer was okay, you answer once. The first time. After that, you say something like, I already answered that one, I think you can sit with it. And then change the subject.
Understood. One answer, then the set phrase. Should I log the number of requests?
Yes, please. That'll help. And there's a second practice interview with the counselor next week, right, Caleb?
Thursday.
Dad doesn't come to that one, and doesn't wait in the building. You go on your own. Okay?
Okay. That one's fine, it's just Ms. Alvarez.
Can I ask something? What do I do Saturday if someone actually does get mad? Like what do I say?
What do you think you'd say?
I don't know. I'd probably just freeze. Or call a manager.

Calling a manager is actually a perfectly normal thing a cashier does. That's what the manager is there for. It's not a failure. What would be a problem is if you went to the back and stayed there, the way you stayed in the bathroom at dinner. Do you see the difference?
One is like, doing the job. The other one is leaving.

Exactly. You can say, let me get my manager, and stand there while they sort it out. That's you staying in it. And most customers on most Saturdays aren't going to get mad at all. They'll want their groceries and they'll go. You'll see.
May I add one observation? He's very good with customers when he's stocking. They ask him where things are all the time. I've seen it when I've stopped in. He's polite, he walks them to the aisle.
That's useful. Caleb, is that true?
I mean, yeah. But that's different. They're not mad. And there's no line.

That's a fair difference, and I'm glad you can name it. A line and someone being upset, that's the part that makes it a five. Saturday you get to find out what that's actually like, instead of guessing. Dad, please don't stop in at the store on Saturday.
Noted. I won't.
And the dinners?
Let's leave the dinners for now. Just keep noticing. We'll come back to that one. Good work today, Caleb.

Dad will call the manager to undo the shelf-only request
A diagnosis such as generalized anxiety disorder, or medication
A Fear Level of 9 or higher for interviews
